title: Break the Anmeldung–bank chicken-and-egg with an online bank
body: Registering your address (Anmeldung) needs a signed lease, yet several traditional German banks want a registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung) before they will open an account — a loop newcomers get stuck in. The common fix is to open an online bank such as N26 first: as All About Berlin notes, 'N26 does not require this document', so 'if you just moved to Germany, and you don't have an apartment yet, you can still open an N26 account', then add your registered address later.

title: Opening an N26 account: a few minutes on your phone with just an ID
body: N26 accounts are opened entirely on a smartphone: you must be over 18, have your own phone and a valid ID, and complete identity verification in a supported language. N26 says opening 'takes just a few minutes' and your virtual Debit Mastercard 'is ready to use immediately', so you have a working account and card while a physical card is posted. The Smart plan is listed at €4.90 per month.

title: Mitte — the central, historic core
body: Mitte is the city's central district and its historic and cultural heart, home to landmarks such as the Berlin Cathedral and the government and museum quarters. Being the geographic centre it is convenient for commuting but also the busiest, most tourist-heavy part of the city.

title: Prenzlauer Berg — quiet streets with a trendy edge
body: Prenzlauer Berg sits within the Pankow borough. The city portal describes it as 'a paradise for families, a playground for hipsters and trendsetters, or just a cozy residential area', reflecting its mix of quiet residential streets and a café-and-boutique scene.

title: Kreuzberg — lively, multicultural inner city
body: Kreuzberg (part of the Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg borough) is one of Berlin's best-known inner-city districts. The city portal presents it as a 'popular district' that draws residents and visitors for its lively, multicultural street life and nightlife.

title: Neukölln — fast-changing and diverse
body: Neukölln is one of Berlin's most rapidly changing inner-city districts; the city portal describes it as caught 'between its working-class past and rapid gentrification'. It is known for a diverse, multicultural population and, in its northern part, a busy bar and food scene.

title: Fare zones: AB covers the city, ABC adds Brandenburg and BER
body: Berlin fares use zones A, B and C sold in combinations. Zone AB covers 'the urban center of Berlin as well as the area up to the city limits' and is what you need for almost all trips inside the city. You only need zone ABC for the surrounding area, which includes BER Airport and Potsdam Central Station.

title: No turnstiles — but buy and validate before you ride
body: Berlin's U-Bahn and S-Bahn have no ticket barriers or turnstiles; it is a proof-of-payment system with random inspections. Buy a ticket before you travel — the free BVG app works — and note that single paper tickets must be validated by stamping them at the yellow or red platform boxes. Riding without a valid ticket means a €60 penalty fare.

title: You must register at your assigned catchment primary school
body: Every Berlin address is assigned a catchment-area primary school (Einzugsbereich); children living there are 'guaranteed a place at the school in their residential area and must always register there first', during the official window about ten months before school starts. You must register at this assigned school even if you plan to use a different or private school. Compulsory schooling begins for children who turn six by 30 September.

title: Bilingual state schools (SESB) alongside private international schools
body: Beyond standard German public schools, Berlin runs public bilingual state schools — the Staatliche Europa-Schulen Berlin (SESB) — which teach in German plus a partner language, a state-funded route to bilingual education. Fee-paying international schools also operate across the city. Either way, you must still register your child at the assigned catchment school first.

title: Health insurance is compulsory — statutory (GKV) vs private (PKV)
body: Health insurance is compulsory in Germany, and most residents are in a statutory health insurance fund (gesetzliche Krankenkasse, GKV). Statutory members 'are entitled to the same benefits', premiums depend on income, and children are co-insured free of charge. Employees earning above an income threshold, plus the self-employed and civil servants, may instead choose private health insurance (PKV).

title: Seeing a Hausarzt — no NHS-style registration, just bring your card
body: There is no formal registration with one GP as in the UK NHS: you simply choose a Hausarzt (family doctor) practice and book an appointment when you need one. Bring your health insurance card (the electronic eGK) so the practice can bill your insurer directly. The Hausarzt is the usual first point of contact and can refer you to specialists, though for many specialties you can also book directly.

title: Anmeldung: 14 days, free, and appointments are scarce
body: You must register your address (Anmeldung) within 14 days of moving in; it is free and done at a Bürgeramt (or online with a BundID/eID). Slots are notoriously hard to find — the city advises checking early in the morning when new appointments are released and selecting all Berlin locations. Missing the two weeks is fine as long as you hold a booked appointment, and you should never buy 'appointments', which the city warns are 'often fraudulent'. Bring your passport/ID and the Wohnungsgeberbestätigung (landlord confirmation).

title: The broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag) is per household
body: Germany charges a broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag) of €18.36 per month per dwelling: 'one dwelling – one fee', regardless of how many people live there or how many devices you own. When you register your new address, the residents' registration office notifies the contribution service, which then writes to you to arrange payment. It is mandatory, so budget for it per household rather than per person.

title: Pfand: get your bottle deposits back at the supermarket
body: Many drink bottles and cans carry a refundable deposit (Pfand) you pay at purchase and reclaim when you return the empties. Single-use (Einweg) plastic bottles and aluminium cans carry a €0.25 deposit; the deposit overall ranges from 8 to 25 cents depending on the container. Return empties to a Pfandautomat (reverse vending machine) at a supermarket entrance — it prints a coupon you redeem at the till.

title: Deutschland-Ticket: €63 a month for nationwide local transport
body: The Deutschland-Ticket is a flat €63 per month monthly subscription that covers all local and regional public transport across the whole of Germany (buses, trams, U-Bahn, S-Bahn and regional trains), not just Berlin. It excludes long-distance IC, EC and ICE trains. For most residents it is the simplest recurring transport cost and adds nationwide regional travel on top of the Berlin network.
